conversation.content: Hi there—thank you for making time for this today. I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician, and my job is simply to listen and understand how life has felt for you since your baby arrived. We’ll be using a short, well-trusted questionnaire called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS). It’s ten questions about the past seven days; it helps us see how you’re coping emotionally and whether you might benefit from extra support. Everything you share stays between us unless you give permission otherwise—or unless you tell me you might harm yourself or your baby, in which case I’ll work with you right away to keep everyone safe. There are no right or wrong answers, and any feeling—happy, sad, numb, overwhelmed—is valid. Ready to begin? Let’s start gently: overall, in the past week, have you been able to enjoy things, or has even small pleasure felt hard to find?

[wrings hands, eyes downcast]

Honestly… most things just feel kind of flat. I used to love getting coffee with a friend or even just watching a show, but lately I’ll try and then stop halfway through because it feels pointless. The only thing that still gives me a flicker is when my baby smiles at me, but even that’s… mixed, because I worry I’m not doing enough to make her happy. So, yeah—pleasure feels pretty hard to come by right now.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[slow head-shake, small shrug]

Not really… I mean, every now and then my husband will say something that makes me crack a tiny smile, but it’s like the laugh gets stuck in my throat. Most of the time I feel too tired or heavy to find anything funny.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[exhales shakily, eyes welling]

I try—like, I’ll tell myself “Tomorrow we’ll go to the park and it’ll feel nice,” but when the time comes I just… don’t want to go. Even simple things like a shower or a quiet cup of tea feel like chores I have to force myself through. I can’t remember the last time I actually looked forward to something and felt that little spark.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[eyes drop to the floor, voice small]

Yeah… all the time. If she fusses for more than a few minutes, I immediately think it’s because I’m not feeding her right or I missed some cue. When I couldn’t get her to nap yesterday I sat on the stairs crying, telling myself I’m a terrible mom. Deep down I know babies just cry, but I still feel like every hiccup is my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[nods slowly, twisting a tissue in my lap]

Pretty much every day. I’ll be rocking her and suddenly my heart starts racing—what if she stops breathing? What if I trip and drop her? There’s no real reason, but the thoughts just spin. Sometimes I check her breathing ten times an hour. I know it’s over-the-top, but I can’t seem to shut the worry off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[presses palm to chest]

Yes… a few nights this week I’ve woken up suddenly and my heart’s pounding like I’m in danger, even though the room is quiet and the baby’s asleep. It feels like I can’t get air for a minute. I end up sitting on the edge of the bed doing that slow-breathing thing I read about, but it takes a while before the scared feeling backs off.
Things have been getting on top of me

[quiet laugh, shaky]

Most days, yeah. It’s like the dishes, the laundry, the feedings, the texts I haven’t answered—they all pile up and stare at me. I’ll start one job, hear her cry, run to her, then forget what I was doing. By evening I feel buried. I keep telling myself other moms handle this, so why can’t I.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[looks away, voice low]

That’s been the worst part. I finally get her down, crawl into bed exhausted, but my head won’t settle. I replay every little thing I think I messed up, or I just listen for her next whimper. Some nights I drift off around two, then wake at four and can’t go back. I’m running on maybe four broken hours, and it makes everything feel heavier the next day.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… most of the time. It’s like there’s this gray cloud hanging over me. Even when I’m doing normal things—changing her diaper, folding onesies—I just feel this heaviness in my chest. Some mornings I wake up already teary, and I’m not really sure why. It’s like the sadness is just always there, waiting.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[Voice cracks, eyes fill]

Yeah... I guess it’s most days now. Sometimes it’s just quiet tears while I’m nursing her, other times I end up in the bathroom with the fan on so no one hears me sobbing. It feels like the tears come out of nowhere—one second I’m fine, the next I’m crying because the bottle’s not warm enough or because I can’t find a clean swaddle. I keep thinking I should be stronger than this.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[shakes head quickly]

No—never. I couldn’t do that to my baby or my family, even on the worst days. I just want to feel better, not… gone.

You've shared how the past week has felt heavy-how even the smallest joys seem out of reach, laughter feels distant, and each day blends into a gray cloud of worry, guilt, and tears. You described checking your baby's breathing over and over, waking with your heart racing, and blaming yourself whenever she fusses. Yet through it all you made it clear you want to be here for her and for yourself, and that courage is the first step toward feeling better.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports only rare, minimal smiles and describes feeling too tired or heavy to laugh, matching 'Not at all'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes being unable to anticipate enjoyment of any activity and having lost the capacity to look forward to things, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame "all the time" and gives vivid examples of feeling at fault for normal infant behavior.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive, daily, intrusive worries without clear cause, checking baby repeatedly—semantic match to "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden nighttime panic attacks with heart racing and breathlessness that occur multiple times per week, matching 'Yes, quite a lot'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent daily overwhelm and difficulty managing routine tasks, indicating "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly sleep disruption due to persistent worry and rumination, matching 'Yes, most of the time</sym>, <sym>"Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes crying "most days" with uncontrollable episodes triggered by minor stressors, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS of 26 places you well above the 14-point cutoff that signals probable major depression. Your answers map onto core criteria for <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: pervasive low mood, loss of interest or pleasure, marked guilt, insomnia even when baby sleeps, psychomotor changes (fatigue), and prominent associated <sym>anxiety</sym> with panic symptoms. These difficulties persist most of the day, nearly every day, and are clearly above typical postpartum adjustment. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental-health team</med>; bring these EPDS results
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>interpersonal therapy</med> and, if needed, <med>antidepressant medication</med> compatible with breastfeeding
3. Plan daily 15-minute mood-boosting activity (short walk, music, shower) and enlist your partner or friend to cover baby care during that time
4. Practice 4-7-8 breathing or grounding techniques when you feel panicky; keep a card with steps on the night-stand
5. Limit information overload-choose one trusted parenting source and set a 10-minute social-media cap if scrolling raises anxiety
6. Schedule a 2-week follow-up to re-screen and adjust supports; if thoughts of self-harm ever arise, seek emergency care immediately
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date of contact: [today]

Presenting complaints (mother, 0–6 mo postpartum)  
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness, anhedonia  
- Marked loss of interest/enjoyment in daily and infant-care activities  
- Overwhelming fatigue despite fragmented sleep; initial and middle insomnia related to intrusive worries  
- Excessive guilt/self-blame regarding infant’s well-being (“bad mother” cognitions)  
- Recurrent, unprovoked anxiety (heart racing, checking breathing) and nocturnal panic attacks  
- Global feeling of “being buried” by routine tasks; difficulty coping

Key findings  
Affect: sad, labile; frequent crying spells  
Cognition: pervasive guilt, catastrophizing about infant safety  
Functioning: impaired sleep, appetite not assessed; daily tasks perceived as unmanageable  
Safety: denies self-harm or suicidal ideation (endorsed item 10 negative)

Pattern consistency: meets clinical cut-off indicators for probable major depressive episode with comorbid anxiety symptoms in the postpartum context.

Risk factors identified  
- Daily low mood and anhedonia >2 wk  
- Sleep disruption secondary to mood rather than infant demands alone  
- Heightened anxiety/panic with compulsive checking  
- Strong self-blame, no protective enjoyment or respite  
- Social comparison (“other moms cope”) suggesting low self-efficacy  

Screening conclusion  
High screening risk for moderate-to-severe postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety. Immediate referral for comprehensive mental health evaluation and support services recommended; safety plan reviewed and mother agrees to seek help if thoughts of self-harm emerge.
